paragraphs.en: The [[train]] came into the [[valley]] late in the afternoon, and I stepped onto the platform with a [[broad]] smile and far too much luggage.
I had left [[Europe]] and a [[city]] job to [[travel]] here, and I did not know how long I would stay.
The last [[transport]] was a bus [[along]] a road that [[followed|follow]] the river for twenty kilometres.
The [[mountain]] rose on both sides, and the [[forest]] above the [[meadow]] was already turning [[brown]].
A rock [[formation]] [[enclosed|enclose]] the village like a pair of hands, and the air was thin enough at this [[altitude]] to make me stop and breathe.
The silence [[amazed|amaze]] me; [[within]] an hour I had forgotten the [[traffic]] of the coast.
My aunt's [[inn]] stood at the end of the lane, a [[simple]] stone house with a [[primitive]] kitchen and a [[rent]] she could no longer afford.
The [[price]] of repairs was more than the [[money]] she had, and I could see [[mold]] (or [[mould]]) on the north wall the moment we went in.
We had to [[remove]] the damp plaster, [[discard]] two rotten beams, and [[clean]] every room before the summer.
It was [[tough]] work and no [[luxury]]: for the first week I slept [[alone]] on a floor of boards.
A builder came to [[inspect]] the roof and told us the work would take a month.
My aunt had been a [[merchant]]'s daughter, and her family had once owned a [[palace]] of a house in the provincial capital.
She was [[fond]] of saying that her grandmother had married an [[aristocrat]] who lost everything, and that the family [[pride]] survived longer than the fortune.
In her [[innermost]] thoughts, she said, she still kept the [[everlasting]] hope of restoring the place.
Her father had belonged to a [[guild]] of tea traders, and a [[pilgrim]] once told him the house would outlive him.
She would [[bring]] the old chairs down from the attic and [[devote]] the rest of her life to it, as if the [[former]] ballroom could hear her.
We drew up a [[budget]] that was [[comprehensive]] and painfully [[exact]].
Every [[digit]] had to be right, and we could not [[foresee]] the cost of cement in a year of [[inflation]].
The project would [[develop]] in three stages, and [[even]] the smallest [[form]] of delay would cost us a month.
I had a little savings, but nothing [[comparable]] to the sum we needed; winning the lottery would have been the only [[jackpot]].
We would [[maximize]] what we could do ourselves and spend [[sparingly]] on the rest.
In June a [[film-making]] crew arrived to [[shoot]] a documentary about the valley, and they asked to use the inn as their base.
None of them were [[amateurs|amateur]]; they had a [[repertoire]] of [[foreign]] festivals behind them, and one had won a [[prize]] in [[Europe]].
Their [[gig]] was small but well paid, and their [[American]] director kept everyone moving with a steady [[prompting]].
The only [[nuisance]] was the equipment: a [[driving]] van and a [[redirected|redirect]] generator that hummed all night.
The whole thing nearly ended as a [[bummer]] when the money ran short, but a sponsor agreed to [[endorse]] the film.
A developer wanted the land next to the inn, and his [[agent]] offered my aunt a [[bribe]].
The [[principal]] of the offer was a new road; the [[principle]] was that no one should be forced to sell.
The developer had [[corrupted]] local officials and tried to [[evade]] tax, and his company was a [[taxpayer]] only on paper.
He filed a [[tort]] claim against us, and the [[filer's|filer]] papers were full of [[private]] details that had nothing to do with the case.
We refused to [[renege]] on our promise to the village, and [[eventually]] the [[transaction]] collapsed.
Every [[intent]] behind his offer was [[deep-seated]] greed, and we were [[affected]] more than we admitted.
The village called a meeting, and a [[clergyman]] opened it with a short [[speech]].
He asked us to [[cite]] [[evidence]] rather than rumour, and to keep the [[moral]] tone of the discussion calm.
A [[plurality]] of the villagers wanted to fight, but the [[crux]] of the matter was money, not anger.
We put a [[sign]] at the gate and agreed on a [[convention]] for how the land could be used.
The minutes were [[altogether]] clear, and [[foremost]] among them was the demand for a public [[report]].
One old man said the issue was not [[insignificant]], and that a village without a centre would not last.
The developer threatened [[prison]] for my aunt, though she was [[innocent]] of any [[evil]].
We could not [[differ]] with the facts, only with the interpretation, and his lawyer was an [[outsider]] who knew nothing of the valley.
The [[side]] of the road he wanted was ours, and [[thus]] the case turned on a single document that a [[thief]] could have taken in a second.
I began to [[pray]] in a way I had not since childhood, not for victory but for a [[clear]] head.
The hearing lasted two days, and the judge asked for patience.
On [[Saturday]] we took the [[trail]] up the [[mountain]], following a [[brochure]] that promised a view of the whole valley.
My [[foot]] slipped once, and I cut my [[belt]] on a stone.
At [[altitude]] the air was thin, and we stopped every hundred metres to [[browse]] the [[sight]] of cloud below us.
The [[sightseeing]] crowd had gone home, and we had the [[meadow]] to ourselves.
From the top the inn looked like a toy, and the [[prize]] for the climb was a silence I have rarely found.
On the way down a stone [[bumped|bump]] the cart, and the [[wire]] rope snapped.
I [[shoved|shove]] my aunt clear and took the [[force]] of the fall on my [[shoulder]].
The [[shock]] of the fall left a [[bruise]] across my arm, and for a [[moment]] I could not [[mount]] the bike again.
A [[tear]] in the tarpaulin let the rain in, and we had to [[clamp]] it shut with a piece of wood.
The [[rescue]] team arrived in a jeep, and a [[parachute]] flare lit the [[wreck]] of the cart.
[[Although]] the forecast was good, the [[temperature]] dropped after dark, and the [[evening]] came in [[dim]].
The brown hills turned grey, and I [[clasped|clasp]] my hands around a cup filled to the [[brim]].
We sat by the fire and said little, and frost began to [[form]] on the window.
In the morning the valley was white, and every [[trait]] of the old landscape was softened.
The village school had one [[class]] for all the [[children]], and twelve pupils of different ages shared a room.
The teacher, a young woman from the [[university]], gave a [[lesson]] on rivers, and her [[ambition]] was to send one of them to college.
Her [[diet]] was simple: a [[bun]] and tea at noon, and [[pork]] twice a month.
The [[outpouring]] of support after the fire was [[similar]] to nothing I had seen in the city.
Children are [[impressionable]], she said, and a good [[event]] can [[inspire]] them for years.
The [[gulf]] between the village and the city was wide, but it was not unbridgeable.
A [[watcher]] from the reserve came to [[scan]] the ridge for [[endangered]] birds.
He said the [[forest]] was full of small life, and that the [[monster]] in local stories was probably a bear.
The [[devil]] is in the details, he added, and the [[crux]] of conservation is not [[ever]] catching the animal but protecting its [[traits|trait]].
His team used a [[probe]] and a camera trap, and the [[fuel]] for the trip cost more than the equipment.
He opened his [[mouth]] to yawn, then laughed at his own enthusiasm.
Back at the inn I read the news: [[inflation]] was at seven [[percent]], and the [[dollar]] had strengthened again.
A [[trillion]] sounds abstract until it reaches a family [[budget]]; then it is a smaller loaf and a colder room.
I tried to [[maximize]] our savings and to [[lessen]] our [[bulk]] purchases, buying rice in small bags.
We were [[insatiable]] for good news, and the [[bubble]] of hope grew while our savings [[shrank|shrink]].
The [[underuse]] of the old barn was a waste, and we decided to turn it into a dining room.
We spent [[sparingly]] and [[accelerated|accelerate]] the work with our own hands.
On [[Monday]] a reporter came to [[print]] a story about the inn, and the piece appeared with a [[negative]] headline.
We could not [[delete]] the article, so we wrote a [[reply]] that was [[responsive]] to each point.
The [[insensitivity]] of the headline hurt more than the facts, and a [[deep-seated]] suspicion of outsiders surfaced again.
I learned to [[browse]] the comments without reading them, and to offer [[insight]] rather than opinion.
[[Specifically]], we asked readers to visit and see the work for themselves, and the [[clicks|click]] on our page doubled.
A [[wire]] service picked up the story, and the [[report]] travelled further than we expected.
On the [[eve]] of opening, we [[shut]] the door and looked at the empty dining room.
It had taken a year, and [[yet]] the building looked as if it had always been this way.
We would [[renew]] the lease and [[build]] a small kitchen garden; [[whenever]] it rained, we would work inside.
The [[watershed]] came when the village voted to protect the land, and the developer sold his option.
[[Meantime]] there was little to [[assuage]] our [[worry]] except work.
The inn would not [[repeat]] its old life, but it could [[evolve]] into something calmer and, [[eventually]], into a kind of [[harmony]].
The [[short]] version of the story is that we stayed.
The longer version is written on the walls, where [[foreign]] guests have left their names.
I do not know whether the [[city]] will call me back, but I have stopped planning my life as a straight line.
[[Whenever]] I am asked why I came, I say that a place can [[shorten]] a person's [[ambition]] and still make him larger.
